NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
The intervention is to implement a pulsed electric field treatment system across the heat exchanger plates to disrupt biofilm formation and scale precipitation. Standard practice relies on periodic mechanical cleaning and/or chemical treatment (chlorination) to control fouling. Our mitigation introduces a fundamentally different mechanism by applying controlled electric pulses that induce electroporation in microbial cells and disrupt crystal lattice formation in scale, preventing their attachment to the metal surfaces. This is distinct from adjacent techniques like electrochemical treatment which continuously generate reactive species, as our approach uses non-chemical, physical disruption mechanisms that don't introduce reactive byproducts. The intervention directly attacks the driving physics of fouling by creating unfavorable conditions for microbial adhesion and mineral nucleation through electrophysical effects rather than relying on biocidal action or mechanical removal.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing physical relation is the electroporation effect on cell membranes and electrocrystallization inhibition. For microbial cells, the electric field strength (E) required for electroporation is approximately 1-10 kV/cm, with the pore formation probability following a sigmoidal relationship with field strength. For scale formation, the electric field disrupts the crystallization kinetics by increasing the activation energy for nucleation, reducing the nucleation rate J by a factor of exp(-ΔG*/kT), where ΔG* is the modified activation energy under the electric field. A 5 kV/cm pulsed field applied across the 2mm plate spacing would induce sufficient electroporation to inactivate >99% of bacteria and reduce calcium carbonate nucleation by >90%, as demonstrated in studies on electrocrystallization inhibition (Matsusaki et al., 2000; Sondhi et al., 2018).

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
Standard Practice Components:
- Mechanical cleaning every 3-6 months
- Chlorination system maintaining <0.5 ppm residual (if used)
- Plate heat exchanger with standard 316L stainless steel plates

Proposed Intervention Components:
1. Pulsed electric field generator unit (b) - replaces chlorination system
2. Electrode plates (a) - installed in existing heat exchanger headers
3. Control system (b) - integrates with existing building automation system
4. Power conditioning unit (b) - mounts adjacent to existing electrical equipment room
5. Insulated wiring harness (c) - routed through existing conduit pathways
6. Operating procedure (c) - modified start-up/shutdown sequence to activate pulsed field during low-flow periods

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
- Equipment: Adds pulsed electric field generator (b), electrode plates (a), control system (b), power conditioning unit (b) - comparable in weight to chlorination system equipment if present
- Installation: Electrode plates utilize existing header space, wiring uses existing conduit - minimal additional labor
- Maintenance: No additional consumables (replacing biocide chemicals), periodic inspection of electrodes (similar to existing heat exchanger inspection frequency)
- Operational: Adds power consumption (~200W continuous for controller + pulsed energy during operation), but eliminates chemical handling and monitoring requirements
- Overall Burden: Same burden class (existing infrastructure can accommodate equipment, no new facility requirements, comparable maintenance frequency)

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: Install pulsed electric field system on test heat exchanger in parallel with identical control unit. Run both units under identical cooling loads for 12 months. Measure heat transfer coefficient and pressure drop weekly. At 12 months, compare performance to baseline (mechanically cleaned state).

Instruments: Heat transfer coefficient measurement via temperature sensors (inlet/outlet) and flow meters; pressure transducers across heat exchanger; biofilm assessment via ATP testing on removable coupons; scale analysis via microscopy on coupons.

Pass/Fail Threshold: Test passes if test unit maintains heat transfer coefficient >2500 W/m2K throughout 12 months without exceeding 20% increase in pressure drop. Control unit must show >30% degradation in heat transfer coefficient or require mechanical cleaning before 12 months.

Duration: 12 months continuous operation with weekly measurements.

Kill Criterion: Test fails immediately if either unit experiences a heat transfer coefficient drop below 2000 W/m2K or if pulsed electric field system requires maintenance more than twice during the test period.
